prompt: A designer wants the planner to look and behave the same on an Android phone and an iPhone. Which of these differences can no design remove, because the system enforces it?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 1.

choices.text: Tabs sit in a bar at the bottom on iOS, while Material also offers tabs at the top
choices.why: That is the two companies' design guides speaking. A designer can follow them or break them, and the app still works.

choices.text: Material draws a floating button for the main action, and iOS puts it in the top bar
choices.why: A convention again. An app can ignore it; users notice, and nothing stops the app from running.

choices.text: Every Android phone has a system back the app must answer, and an iPhone has none
choices.why: Back belongs to the system on Android: the app cannot remove it, only decide what it does. On an iPhone going back is a control the app draws.

choices.text: Lists and switches look different on Android and on an iPhone, drawn by each system's own parts
choices.why: They look different by convention, and an app that draws its own can make them look alike. The look is a guide, not a rule the system enforces.

prompt: A new iOS release restyles every switch. The planner exists in three builds: React Native, Flutter, and a WebView wrapper. Which build shows the new switch without a new release of the app?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 2.

choices.text: The React Native build, since at runtime its components become the platform's own views
choices.why: React Native creates the corresponding iOS view for each component, so a switch is the system's switch and changes when the system changes.

choices.text: The Flutter build, because Impeller paints its widgets in the style of the current system
choices.why: Flutter bypasses the system's widgets and draws its own pixels, so a new system look reaches it only after Flutter and the app are updated.

choices.text: The wrapper, because its WebView is part of the system and is updated together with it
choices.why: The WebView renders the page, and a switch in it is whatever the page's CSS made it. A new system style does not rewrite that CSS.

choices.text: No build: a new look reaches an app once it is rebuilt with the new release's own SDK
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite of the platform's views: they look like the system's and change with it, with no new release of the app.

prompt: The planner saves a half-typed session in the clean-up code that runs when the app closes. In testing, closing the app by hand always saves it. Which student loses the draft?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 4.

choices.text: One who answers a short call in the middle of typing and comes straight back to the planner
choices.why: A call pauses and stops the app without killing it, so everything in memory is still there when she returns.

choices.text: One whose phone is short of memory, and whose app the system kills while it is suspended
choices.why: A kill in the background sends no callback on any platform, so the clean-up never runs. The save belongs on the way to the background.

choices.text: One who swipes the planner away on purpose, because closing it by hand skips every clean-up
choices.why: Closing by hand is the case where those clean-ups do run, which is exactly why the test passed and the bug survived.

choices.text: Nobody: before freeing an app's memory the system calls it one last time so it can save
choices.why: There is no goodbye. The move to suspended is silent, and so is the kill; the app hears nothing after entering the background.

prompt: To avoid any lookup after a restore, the planner saves the whole open course, with all its sessions, in the screen's saved state. What does lesson 5 say goes wrong?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 5.

choices.text: Saved state is cleared whenever the system kills the process, so the course is lost just the same
choices.why: Saved state is the option that does survive a kill by the system. What it does not survive is the user closing the screen on purpose.

choices.text: Only Android has a problem, since iOS sets no limit and the object comes back exactly as saved
choices.why: Apple gives no number and still asks for lightweight data, warning against model data there. And a stale copy is wrong on every platform.

choices.text: An id can point at a course deleted meanwhile, so saving the object is the safer of the two
choices.why: A missing course behind an id fails where the app can see it and handle it. A saved copy draws an old object as if it were current.

choices.text: It grows with each session, and a course renamed elsewhere comes back with its old title
choices.why: Ids stay at 80 bytes whatever the plan holds, while the whole plan passed 150 KB and Android recommends under 50 KB. And a copy can be stale by the time it is read.

prompt: An Android phone's screen is 400 dpi, a density that sits in no bucket. How many physical pixels wide is a 56 dp button on it?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 7.

prompt: The planner shows its course list and a course's detail side by side only in a window at least expanded wide and not compact tall. With Android's breakpoints, match each window, in dp, to what the planner shows.
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 8.

pairs.right: expanded width, compact height: one pane

prompt: The planner reads the screen's insets once, at launch, in portrait, and pads its list by them. Ana turns the phone sideways, and the first letters of every row vanish under the camera's cutout. Why?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 9.

choices.text: The list was padded twice, once by hand and once by the toolkit, which pushed it under the notch
choices.why: Padding twice moves content further from the edge and leaves a gap. It cannot slide anything under a cutout.

choices.text: Insets are counted in physical pixels, so on a dense screen the padding came out too small
choices.why: Insets are layout sizes in dp or points, like any other size in lesson 7. A pixel count is never what the app is given.

choices.text: In landscape the notch sits at one side, and the saved numbers describe the phone as held upright
choices.why: Insets change while the app runs: in landscape the cutout moves and the top inset often disappears. An app that keeps the launch numbers pads the wrong edges.

choices.text: A landscape window has no safe area, so the system expects the app to draw everything edge to edge
choices.why: A safe area exists in every orientation; it simply moves when the phone turns. Only the background is meant to reach the edges.

prompt: From Android 13, why must an app say in advance whether it will handle back itself on the screen being shown, instead of reacting when the back event arrives?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 10.

choices.text: Because the app does not draw the back control, so it has no way to tell when the student pressed it
choices.why: Back is the system's on Android, but the app has always been told about it and decided what it does. The reason for declaring early is newer.

choices.text: Because the back swipe shows where it leads while the finger moves, before the gesture is committed
choices.why: Predictive back shrinks the current screen over the one behind it during the swipe. Showing the right one means knowing who answers before the gesture is committed.

choices.text: Because since Android 12 back at the root kills the app, and the system needs the app's consent first
choices.why: Back at the root of the task moves it to the background, as Home does. Nothing is killed by it.

choices.text: Because iOS demands the same declaration for its edge swipe, and Android adopted the rule for both
choices.why: On an iPhone going back is a control the app draws, with the swipe as its shortcut. There is no system back to declare anything to.

prompt: The planner asks for notifications when a student first taps "remind me", and plans to show its own screen explaining reminders only if the student says no. What does that plan cost on an iPhone?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 12.

choices.text: The explanation arrives too late: on iOS the first no is final, so it has to come before the one dialog
choices.why: iOS shows the dialog once and stores the answer. An explanation shown after a refusal leads to no second dialog, only to Settings.

choices.text: Nothing: after the app's own screen, iOS shows its dialog a second time, exactly as Android does
choices.why: That is Android's rule, and only once. On iOS later requests do not prompt the person again.

choices.text: The plan breaks a rule: only the system may explain a permission, so the app's own screen is refused
choices.why: The explanation belongs to the app. What it must never do is imitate the system's dialog or record a yes by itself.

choices.text: The moment is wrong: iOS expects every permission to be requested together during the first launch
choices.why: The first launch is the worst moment on both platforms. The tap on "remind me" is the right one, because it explains itself.

prompt: The planner's link parser ignores the `?from=email` on a link to the week. Marketing now wants the tag sent to the server and kept, to see which newsletter brings students back. What changes?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 13.

choices.text: Nothing: the student never typed the tag, so it is not data about them and no store form asks for it
choices.why: Where somebody came from is data about them, which is what makes it useful to marketing. Kept on a server, it is collected.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the purpose is analytics, because data for the app's own analytics need not be declared
choices.why: Analytics is one purpose on the list, not an exemption. Apple's page says data collected even for the app's own functioning still has to be declared.

choices.text: It becomes tracking, so iOS must first show the App Tracking Transparency prompt to every student
choices.why: Tracking means linking the data with other companies' apps or websites for advertising, or passing it to a broker. Counting your own newsletter is neither.

choices.text: The tag now leaves the phone and is kept, so it is a new inventory line, and the forms must declare it
choices.why: Collected means sent off the device and kept. A tag says where a person came from, and counting that is a new line in the inventory, with a reason somebody has to be willing to write.

prompt: Lesson 15's `batch.ts` is run with one more strategy: poll every 15 seconds. With the model's own constants, how many minutes a day does it count the radio as awake?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 15.

prompt: The planner writes its green, `#2F6F4E`, its spacing steps and its body size once, in one file, and builds both platforms' themes from it. Lesson 18 calls each of those named decisions a design ___.
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 18.

prompt: The planner's week shows seven session rows, each with a tick that marks it done, and a drawing beside the week's total that adds no information. Which of these follow lesson 19? Choose all that apply.
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 19.

choices.text: Each row is one element read as a sentence, labelled with its course and day, such as "Mark SQL on Friday done"
choices.why: Grouped, the row is one swipe instead of three or four, and the course and the day make every label different from the others.

choices.text: Each tick is labelled "green tick icon", so a student who cannot see it knows what is on screen
choices.why: That describes pixels the student cannot see and says nothing about what a double tap does. A label names the purpose.

choices.text: Each tick is labelled "mark done button", so that its role is never missed by the screen reader
choices.why: The role is already announced, so the student hears "button" twice. The label should not repeat it.

choices.text: The decoration next to the total is hidden from the screen reader, so it costs the student no swipe
choices.why: Decoration says nothing and is excluded, out of respect for the student's time, in both platforms' guidance.

choices.text: All seven ticks carry the same label, "mark done", so the screen sounds consistent from row to row
choices.why: Seven identical labels are seven identical sounds. Android's documentation asks for each description to be unique.

prompt: Build 42 of the planner's version 1.10.0 is rejected in review. Ana fixes the bug and uploads the app again, still named 1.10.0. Which build number may the new upload carry?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 20.

choices.text: 42 again, since a build that was rejected never became a release and so used up nothing
choices.why: The build number counts every build that reached the store. Nobody outside the team saw 42, and it is still gone for good.

choices.text: Any number, because the stores compare the version name, and 1.10.0 has not changed
choices.why: It is the other way round: the name is what people read, and the build number is what the store compares and refuses to reuse.

choices.text: 43 or higher: 42 has reached the store, and a build number once used there never comes back
choices.why: Every build that reaches the store spends its number, and the next one must be higher. The name may stay 1.10.0, as in the lesson's figure.

choices.text: 1.10.1, because a fixed build has to carry a higher version name before any store accepts it
choices.why: A rebuild may keep its name with a new build number; the lesson's check passes 1.9.2 rebuilt as build 43.

prompt: `fetchWeek` from lesson 14 is called with `retries: 2`, and its first attempt meets each of the answers below. After which of them does it send the request again? Choose all that apply.
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 14; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: `429 Too Many Requests`, with a `Retry-After` header saying how long to wait
choices.why: 429 is a 4xx, and `fetchWeek` throws anything under 500 at once. Honouring `Retry-After` would need code it does not have.

choices.text: `401 Unauthorized`, because the student's sign-in has expired on the server
choices.why: A 4xx fails the same way however often it is asked. A 401 wants new credentials, not the same request again.

choices.text: `503 Service Unavailable`, from a server that is overloaded for a moment
choices.why: A 5xx says the server failed and might not next time, so the client waits its backoff and tries again.

choices.text: No answer, until `AbortSignal.timeout` stops the attempt with a `TimeoutError`
choices.why: `fetch` rejects, and nothing in the loop catches it, so the error leaves `fetchWeek` at once. Only an answered 5xx is retried.

choices.text: `502 Bad Gateway`, from a proxy whose server behind it answered with nonsense
choices.why: Any status of 500 or more is retried while attempts remain; the first digit says the problem is on the server's side.

prompt: After lesson 14's table, Ana changes "add a session" from a `POST` to `/sessions` into a `PUT` to `/sessions/<id>`, where the app makes up the id once and sends the same one on every attempt. The request times out. May the app send it again?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6; Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 14.

choices.text: Yes: putting the same thing at the same address twice leaves one of it, which is the job the idempotency key did
choices.why: `PUT` replaces whatever is at the address, so doing it twice is doing it once. The id chosen once by the app plays the part of the idempotency key.

choices.text: No: a request that changes something may be repeated only with a separate idempotency key sent beside it
choices.why: The key is a way for the server to recognise a repeat. An address the app chose once does the same job, and `PUT` promises the rest.

choices.text: No: `PUT` stops being idempotent when the answer is lost, because the server may have already stored it
choices.why: Idempotent means a second time leaves the world as the first left it. That holds whether or not the first answer came back.

choices.text: Yes, and the id adds nothing: a `PUT` to `/sessions` would be just as safe, since the method alone decides
choices.why: `PUT` puts this thing at this address. Without one address per session there is nothing for it to replace, and a repeat has nowhere to land twice.

prompt: Ana walks out of the house while the planner is loading the week, Wi-Fi hands over to mobile data, and the request dies halfway. A teammate says HTTP/3 would have helped. What do the two lessons say?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6; Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 14.

choices.text: Nothing would change: methods, codes and headers are the same in every version of HTTP
choices.why: The meanings did not change, and that is the point of the versions section. The transport underneath did, and that is what a handover breaks.

choices.text: It would help: HTTP/3 does not tie a connection to address and port, so the move cannot drop it
choices.why: A TCP connection is tied to the addresses at each end, and a new network means a new address. HTTP/3's transport is not, so the request can carry on.

choices.text: It would help, because HTTP/3 runs over UDP, which keeps no connection, and so has nothing to lose
choices.why: UDP is only the disguise. HTTP/3's protocol on top of it is a connection, with its own ordering and encryption setup.

choices.text: HTTP/2 already does this: many exchanges share one connection, so losing one network loses no request
choices.why: Sharing one connection is about queueing, not about surviving a move. An HTTP/2 connection still dies with the address it was opened from.

prompt: To let a staging domain in, a teammate replaces the parser's whole-host comparison in `links.ts` with `url.host.startsWith("planner.example.com")`. Which link does the parser now accept that it refused before?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8; Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 11.

choices.text: `http://planner.example.com/course/sql`, since the host now matches whatever the scheme is
choices.why: The scheme is checked before the host: an `http:` link still falls through to the refusal, because a verified link is only ever `https`.

choices.text: `https://www.planner.example.com/course/sql`, since `www` is just another subdomain of the planner
choices.why: That host starts with `www.`, not with `planner.`, so the new test refuses it too. `www` is an ordinary subdomain, and a different name.

choices.text: `https://planner.example.net/course/sql`, since the first letters of the two hosts are almost the same
choices.why: "Almost" is not a prefix: `planner.example.net` does not start with `planner.example.com`, and is still refused.

choices.text: `https://planner.example.com.attacker.net/course/sql`, which only `attacker.net` controls
choices.why: A name is read from the right, and every label left of `attacker.net` is whatever its owner invents. Comparing the host whole is what refused it.

prompt: The planner's wrapper build loads a megabyte of script into its WebView. On a modest phone the download finishes quickly, and then for about a second the week does not scroll and taps do nothing. What is the phone doing?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 10; Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: Waiting for the page's `load` event, which holds back every frame until each image and font has arrived
choices.why: The week is on screen already; it is the response that is missing. And `load` is a signal scripts wait for, not a gate on drawing.

choices.text: Drawing each frame about a second late, so the list follows the finger slowly but still moves
choices.why: A frame that misses its slot is not shown late; it is not shown at all. The screen keeps the old picture.

choices.text: Parsing, compiling and running the script on the thread that handles the page, losing every frame
choices.why: A downloaded script costs processing before it runs, on the same thread that answers input. Held for a second, that thread drops about sixty frames at 60 Hz.

choices.text: Still receiving the script, because the phone's link is shared and the last bytes trickle in slowly
choices.why: The download had finished. What a script costs to run is a separate number from what it costs to fetch, and this is the first.

prompt: A teammate proposes that the planner's server keep each phone's IP address and connect to it when a session is about to start, instead of using FCM or APNs. What do the two lessons say against it?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 17; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 4.

choices.text: An IP address is personal data the server may not keep, which is why the platforms replaced it with a token
choices.why: The token is an address the push service understands, not a privacy measure. The problem with the plan is that nothing would arrive.

choices.text: A packet arriving unasked finds no row in the router's NAT table, so the phone must keep a connection open to the push service
choices.why: Nothing outside can start a conversation through NAT. That is why each platform keeps one connection from the phone outwards, and your server hands its message to that service.

choices.text: It would work on Wi-Fi, where the phone has an address of its own, and fail only on mobile data
choices.why: A home router does NAT too: the house shares one public address, and the phone's is private. The phone also moves between networks and sleeps.

choices.text: The server could reach the phone, but each connection keeps the radio awake, so the platforms batch them
choices.why: Battery is part of why the platform shares one connection, but the plan fails earlier: your server cannot reach a phone at all.

prompt: The planner's sign-in token is the signed, self-contained kind from Web lesson 7, and a teammate has stored it in the app's preferences file. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 16; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: Anyone reading the file sees the student's id and the token's expiry, with no key needed
choices.why: Signed is not encrypted: the claims are an encoding, readable by anybody holding the token.

choices.text: The sandbox encrypts the preferences file, so only the planner itself can make sense of the token
choices.why: The sandbox keeps other apps out and encrypts nothing. Preferences are text, as readable as `prefs.json` was to `cat`.

choices.text: A copy taken from the file keeps working until it expires, whatever the server would like
choices.why: A token is checked against its signature, not against a table, so there is nothing to delete. It lasts until its expiry.

choices.text: The preferences file goes into the phone's cloud backup together with the rest of the app's data
choices.why: Auto Backup takes shared preferences by default, and iCloud Backup takes the app's container except the caches. A secret should not travel.

choices.text: Because the token is signed, a copy is useless on any phone other than the one it was issued to
choices.why: The signature stops the token being changed, not being used. Whoever holds it acts as the student.

prompt: Bruno wants the planner to ask the server for changes every minute. "Each check moves 300 bytes, and phones get 50 Mbps now, so it costs nothing." What do the two lessons answer?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 15; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 3.

choices.text: He is wrong about bandwidth: it is shared with the street, so the 300 bytes take far longer to arrive
choices.why: Sharing makes bandwidth a ceiling, not a promise, but the size of the transfer is not where this habit costs.

choices.text: He is right: at that bandwidth the transfer ends in microseconds, and the radio drops to standby with it
choices.why: The radio does not drop when the transfer ends. It stays up for seconds afterwards, because waking it again is slow.

choices.text: He is wrong about latency: each check waits a full round trip, and the waiting is what drains the battery
choices.why: Latency decides how long a check takes, not what it costs the battery. The expensive part is waking the radio at all.

choices.text: Bandwidth only shortens the transfer; every check wakes the radio, which stays up for seconds after it
choices.why: The cost of a sync is mostly the cost of waking up for it. In lesson 15's model, once a minute is 1,440 wake-ups and 432 minutes awake a day.

prompt: An app waits on its main thread for a request to its server: a new TCP connection, no TLS, address already known, and a round trip of 100 ms. The server answers at once. Counting the handshake as Web lesson 2 draws it, how many frames does a 120 Hz screen lose while the app waits?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 6; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 2.

prompt: When the server cannot be reached, the planner's week screen shows the copy it kept, with its age. Which `Cache-Control` directive asks a CDN to behave the same way for a web page?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7; Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 14.

choices.text: `stale-if-error`: when the origin is broken, serve the old copy rather than an error
choices.why: That is the stale state at a larger scale. The difference is the age: the week screen says how old its copy is, and a CDN tells the visitor nothing.

choices.text: `stale-while-revalidate`: serve the old copy at once and fetch a new one in the background
choices.why: That serves the old copy even when the origin is fine. The week screen asks first, with a deadline, and falls back only when that fails.

choices.text: `no-cache`: keep the copy, and ask the origin every time before using it for anybody
choices.why: `no-cache` means ask before every use. It says nothing about what to serve when the origin cannot answer, which is the case the week screen covers.

choices.text: `max-age=7200`: use the copy for two hours without asking anybody, and check after that
choices.why: A fresh copy is used without any request at all, healthy origin or not. The week screen never skips asking.

prompt: A course app wants to push "You scored 4 out of 10 in the SQL test". A teammate says it is safe, "because our server sends it to FCM and APNs over HTTPS". What do the two lessons say?
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 17; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: Safe, because the service's valid certificate proves that whoever runs it treats the student's data properly and lawfully
choices.why: A certificate proves who controls a name, nothing more. It says nothing about what happens to the data on the other side.

choices.text: Not safe: HTTPS hides it from the path, but Google's or Apple's service reads it, and it lands on a lock screen
choices.why: Encryption protects the conversation, not what the far end does with it, and the far end is the push service. Apple's guidelines say not to push sensitive information; send "you have a new message".

choices.text: Safe if the push carries data and nothing to show, which travels outside Google's and Apple's servers
choices.why: A data-only message shows nothing on screen, but it takes the same road through the platform's service, and it is the less reliable kind.

choices.text: Not safe, because a message with a score in it is too large for the 4,096 bytes a push may carry
choices.why: That sentence is a few dozen bytes. Size limits what a push can carry, not what it should.

prompt: The planner asks `https://api.planner.example.com/week` for the first time today, with nothing cached. Put the stages of that request in order.
hint: Mobile Development Fundamentals, lesson 14; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.
items: The name `api.planner.example.com` is turned into an address
A TCP connection is opened to that address
TLS is negotiated, and the server presents its certificate
The request `GET /week` is sent
The first byte of the answer arrives
The rest of the body is read
trap: The likeliest slip is putting the certificate after the request. The connection is negotiated before any HTTP is spoken, which is why the request itself is already encrypted.

prompt: A frame carrying the planner's `GET /week` reaches the server's network card. Put what the server opens in order, from the first envelope to the request itself.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 5.
items: The frame, with the two MAC addresses and a check at its end
The packet, with the source and destination addresses and a hop count
The segment, with the two ports and the place in the stream
The request text that the application wrote
trap: The likeliest slip is listing the wraps in the order they were put on. At the far end they come off in the opposite order, so the outermost, the frame, is opened first.

prompt: Before the planner can connect, its question about `api.planner.example.com` usually travels in plain text, over UDP, to port ___ of the resolver, which is why anybody on the path can see every name the phone looks up.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8.

prompt: The planner's website moves behind a CDN. Which of these get faster for a student far from the origin? Choose all that apply.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 9.

choices.text: The public course pages, which are the same for every visitor
choices.why: Identical for everybody, so the nearest edge can keep a copy and answer in milliseconds.

choices.text: A search page that takes the origin two seconds to build
choices.why: A CDN moves copies closer; it has no opinion about how long the origin takes. Two seconds stay two seconds.

choices.text: The student's own week, a page that is marked `private`
choices.why: A personal page must not be stored at the edge, so it still travels to the origin, now with an extra hop.

choices.text: The scripts and images with hashed names, kept for a year
choices.why: A fingerprinted file can be cached on machines you do not control for as long as its name lasts, which is what an edge is for.

choices.text: The first visit to the site's name, while its DNS lookup is cold
choices.why: The lookup happens before any connection, in front of the CDN, which can do nothing about it.

prompt: Match each arrangement on the planner's web page to what the browser does with it.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 10.

pairs.left: `<script src="app.js">` in the head, with no attribute
pairs.right: parsing stops while the script is fetched and run

pairs.left: `<script src="app.js" defer>` in the head
pairs.right: fetched during parsing, run after it, in document order

pairs.left: `<script src="stats.js" async>`
pairs.right: run the moment it arrives, wherever the parser has got to

pairs.left: `defer` on a script written inline in the page
pairs.right: ignored, because the script has already arrived

pairs.left: code that waits for `DOMContentLoaded`
pairs.right: runs once the tree is built and deferred scripts have run

right_distractors: runs only once every image and font has finished
fetched only after parsing ends, then run in order

prompt: Ana is chasing a bug in the planner's sign-in form, which submits and then redirects. In the network panel the rows vanish each time the page navigates. The control that keeps them across a navigation is called "___ log".
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 11.

prompt: The planner keeps a 3 MB database, a small settings file and a 24 MB PDF of notes the person downloaded, none of them in a cache folder: 27.01 MB in all. The same build runs on Android and on iOS. What does each phone's backup do with it?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 1.

choices.text: Android backs up nothing, being over its 25 MB quota; iOS backs up all of it, the PDF included
choices.why: Android's quota is all or nothing: past 25 MB the backup is not made. iOS has no quota per app and leaves out only caches and scratch files, so the person pays for 24 MB that could be downloaded again.

choices.text: Android backs up its first 25 MB, the database among them, and iOS leaves the PDF out because it is over the size it allows for one file
choices.why: Android does not take the first 25 MB: past the quota it takes none of it. And iOS sets no limit per file or per app; the person's iCloud storage is the only one.

choices.text: Both back up the database and the settings and skip the PDF, since each system recognises a downloaded document as one it can fetch again
choices.why: Neither system knows where a file came from. They decide by folder, leaving out only the cache and scratch folders, so the app has to put the PDF there or mark it itself.

choices.text: iOS backs up nothing, because the free tier of iCloud is 5 GB per app, and Android backs up everything except what sits in the cache folder
choices.why: The 5 GB free tier is for everything the person owns, not an allowance per app. And here it is Android whose 25 MB quota drops the whole backup.

prompt: The planner's `load` returns `{}` when its settings file does not exist. A teammate wants it to return `{}` as well when `JSON.parse` throws, so that the app never crashes on start. What does the lesson say is wrong with that?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 2.

choices.text: Nothing: a damaged file and a missing one both mean the app has never saved a single setting, so an empty store is the truth in either case
choices.why: Only the missing file means that. A file that exists and does not parse was written once and damaged since, by a torn write for instance.

choices.text: A file that does not parse means something went wrong, and `{}` quietly resets the person's settings to the defaults, with no record
choices.why: A missing file means nothing was saved yet, and empty is the truth. A damaged one is an error for the caller to decide about, which is why DataStore raises an exception of its own and makes an app ask to start over.

choices.text: It hides the parse error, and the real fix is to write the file in place more often, so a damaged copy is soon overwritten
choices.why: Writing in place is what tears a file to begin with. The fix for tearing is to write beside the file and rename; the fix for `load` is to let the error reach the caller.

choices.text: It is fine as long as every save renames a temporary file over the real one, since the rename brings the old settings back on the next launch
choices.why: A rename protects the copy that is about to be replaced. It cannot bring settings back once `load` has handed the app an empty store and the app has saved over them.

prompt: A test of the planner's store, run through `better-sqlite3`, proves that `REFERENCES` refuses a session naming a course that does not exist. Ana tries the same insert by hand in the `sqlite3` shell, on the same file, and it is accepted. What explains it?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 3; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 8.

choices.text: The shell is an older SQLite whose file format ignores `REFERENCES`, so the test and the shell are reading two different schemas
choices.why: The shell's version and the library's may differ, but the file format is the same and either opens what the other wrote. The difference is a setting of the connection.

choices.text: The test used `better-sqlite3` on a database held in memory, and SQLite enforces constraints only on a file on disk
choices.why: The lesson's batch had its `CHECK` enforced in a database held in memory. Where a database lives does not decide what it checks.

choices.text: Foreign keys are checked only on a connection that turns them on, which `better-sqlite3` does and the shell does not
choices.why: The constraint is in the schema either way, and whether it is enforced is a setting of the connection. Two tools on one file can then disagree, a parity gap of the kind the testing course warns about.

choices.text: `REFERENCES` is checked only inside a transaction, and the shell commits each statement on its own, outside any
choices.why: A transaction decides whether several writes land together, not which constraints are checked. The shell accepted the row because its connection had foreign keys off.

prompt: The planner keeps each course's session count on the course row, updated by the app's own code when a session is added or resized. Coverage of that code is 100%, branches included, and every test is green; yet after a session is removed, the course list still counts it. Why did the coverage report not point at the bug?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 4; Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 4.

choices.text: Branch coverage was on and did report the missing arc, but the team read only the total percentage at the bottom
choices.why: An arc is a way out of a decision that exists in the code. No decision in this code mentions a removal, so there is no arc to report.

choices.text: The tests ran the update lines under a double that does nothing, so those lines were counted without being checked
choices.why: That gap is real, a line run under a double is counted and checked by nobody, but here the update for a removal is not a line at all.

choices.text: The count is right inside the transaction and wrong only after the commit, which no test can observe
choices.why: The stored count was never changed by the removal at all. Triggers fix it because they run on every delete, whichever code path made it.

choices.text: The bug is an update nobody wrote, and coverage reports only lines that exist
choices.why: Coverage says which code no test executed. The removal has no line keeping the count, so nothing is marked as missed; a test that recomputes the counts from the sessions after a removal is what finds the drift.

prompt: On every push, the planner's pipeline builds a version 3 database, migrates it to version 4 and compares its schema with a fresh install. It is green, and phones that skipped updates fail at launch with `no such column: synced`. What should the test do instead?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 5; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5.

choices.text: Keep starting from a version 3 database, which most phones run, and have the app retry the migration at its next launch
choices.why: A retry runs the same missing step again and fails again. The phones that fail are exactly the ones not on version 3.

choices.text: Build a database at each shipped version, with a row in its shape, migrate, and compare schema and rows with a fresh install
choices.why: A phone can arrive from any earlier version, so the starting version is an axis production really varies on, like the time zone of the testing course's matrix. The rows matter too: a matching schema says nothing about whether the ticks survived.

choices.text: Start from every version, but compare only the schema with a fresh install, because the rows are the person's data and not the migration's
choices.why: The lesson printed the rows of each path on purpose: a migration that built the right tables and lost the ticks would pass a schema comparison.

choices.text: Run the same test against more versions of SQLite, because `no such column` is a difference of dialect between engines
choices.why: The column is missing because step 3, which creates it, never ran on those phones. What differs is the path between versions, not the engine.

prompt: Version 4 of the planner app ships a migration step that copies some data wrongly, and it has already committed, inside its transaction, on thousands of phones. For its web service the team would run its rollback script. What do the two courses point to here?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 5; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11.

choices.text: Publish version 3 again, so that every phone goes back to running the code that matched the shape of its data
choices.why: The phones' databases are already at version 4, and going back to older code returns the code and nothing else. Version 3 would open a file in a shape it does not know.

choices.text: Correct step 4 where it is and release again, since every phone runs the steps from its own version up to the last one
choices.why: Phones already at version 4 start after step 4, so they never run the corrected one. That is why a shipped step is never edited.

choices.text: Fix it forward, with a step 5 in the next release that repairs the data, because step 4 has run and a shipped step is never edited
choices.why: A phone that ran step 4 will not run it again, so only a later step reaches it. And going back would move code, never data: an older app would meet a database it was not written for.

choices.text: Turn on the library's destructive fallback for one release, so that every phone starts empty and pulls all of its data again from the server
choices.why: Deleting the database deletes what the person wrote offline and the server never received. The safe order is to send what is unsent, then rebuild.

prompt: The history screen pages its sessions by key, asking for the 50 rows after the last date it showed, with an index on `date` alone. Many sessions share a date. What goes wrong, and what does the lesson add?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 6.

choices.text: `date` alone cannot mark where a page ends; ordering by `(date, id)` makes each position unique
choices.why: Keyset paging needs an order no two rows share. The `id` breaks every tie, and the row value `(date, id) > (?, ?)` is answered from the index.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong, because a keyset page starts where the last one ended whatever changed before it, so ties cannot matter
choices.why: That holds for rows a sync inserts earlier in the list. It does not help when the place a page ended is itself ambiguous, which a shared date makes it.

choices.text: Each page walks every row with that date, so the fix is to go back to `OFFSET`, which counts the rows exactly
choices.why: An offset counts by visiting rows, the cost keyset paging removes, and a row arriving from a sync shifts it so that a row is shown twice.

choices.text: The query runs on the main thread whenever several dates tie, so the fix is to move it to a worker that answers later
choices.why: Which thread waits is a separate question from where a page ends. A worker would return the same wrong page without the stutter.

prompt: A teammate replaces the planner's three sync states with one boolean, `dirty`, set on every change and cleared after a successful send. What does that lose?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 7.

choices.text: Nothing: `dirty` and clean are `pending` and `synced`, and a refusal can be shown in a banner at the very moment it happens
choices.why: The refusal arrives during a sync, often long after the person typed the session. With nowhere in the row to keep it, nothing can show it later.

choices.text: The time each row was synced, so the next pull can no longer tell which rows to ask the server for
choices.why: What to pull is the job of the cursor, kept per device. What the boolean loses is the third state, refused, not a time.

choices.text: The rule that screens read the database, since a screen now has to ask the network what state a row is in
choices.why: The boolean still lives in the local database and the screen still reads it there. What goes missing is the difference between waiting and refused.

choices.text: The difference between waiting and refused: a session the server turned down is retried for ever and looks merely slow
choices.why: A refusal is an answer, and the row has to keep it, with the server's reason beside it, so the screen can say which session failed and why.

prompt: Match each test of the planner to the layer of the test pyramid it belongs to.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 1; Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 8.

pairs.left: the coalescing rules, called on a list of operations held in memory
a session and its outbox row, written to a real SQLite file and read back together
the server started on a free port and sent a 300-minute session over HTTP, which it answers with a 422
the product owner's sentence, “a session typed offline is on the week at once”, checked through the app's commands

prompt: The planner's outbox is compacted before each drain. Bia wants one test that would catch any wrong rule somebody adds to the compaction later. Which test fits what both courses say?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 3; Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 8.

choices.text: A table of every pair of operations with the expected result, kept as a CSV the product team can review
choices.why: A table checks the cases somebody wrote down. A wrong rule added later fails only if its case is already a row, and the bug may need a sequence of three.

choices.text: A test that the compacted queue is always shorter than the original, since fewer operations are the point of coalescing
choices.why: A rule that drops a needed update also shortens the queue. Fewer operations is the benefit; the same final state is the correctness.

choices.text: A property-based test that the compacted and the whole queue leave the server in the same state
choices.why: The outbox lesson names the rule every coalescing rule must keep, the same final state. A library that generates inputs finds the sequence nobody thought of, and shrinks it to the smallest that fails.

choices.text: A mock server with `assert_called_once_with` for each request the drain sends after the compaction
choices.why: That restates today's calls, and it breaks on a correct rule that sends fewer of them. The behaviour to check is what the server ends up holding.

prompt: Bia tests the planner's outbox drain with test doubles. Match each thing she passes in to the kind of double it is.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 2; Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 8.

pairs.left: a server set up to answer 503 three times and then 201, for the retry test
a list whose `push` is passed in as the drain's logger, and read after the run
an in-memory server that keeps the sessions it accepted and answers `GET` with them
`null` for the retry policy, in a test that an empty outbox sends nothing
a double built from the HTTP client's real class, checked afterwards for never having been called

prompt: To prove the planner's retry can never create a session twice, Caio's test uses a stub server that answers every `POST` with 201 at once, and asserts the retry loop stops after one attempt. It passes. What has it not covered?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 2; Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 9.

choices.text: Nothing: one 201 and one attempt prove that the client never sends the same session to the server a second time, whatever happens
choices.why: When an answer arrives every time there is never a retry, so the test cannot see what a retry does. The duplicate needs a lost answer.

choices.text: The case that duplicates, a save whose answer is lost, which needs a fake that remembers and a count of what it holds
choices.why: A stub has no memory, so it cannot say how many sessions exist. The duplicate appears only when the work was done and the answer lost, and the client retries as it should.

choices.text: A slow server: the stub should wait past the client's timeout, and the test should then assert that the client gave up
choices.why: A timeout is part of the story, but a server that is merely slow and saves nothing shows only that the client gives up. The harm is a save whose answer never arrives.

choices.text: A 422, since a session the server refused is the case in which the client ends up sending the same bytes twice
choices.why: A 422 is an answer and is not retried at all. The repeated request is the one that went unanswered after it was saved.

prompt: The planner retries a 503 with exponential backoff. A teammate argues the pipeline should do the same with a failing test: run it up to three times and count a pass on any try as green. What do the two courses say?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5; Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 9.

choices.text: A 503 says nothing about the request; a red test is an answer about the code, and retrying it turns flaky tests green
choices.why: The testing course forbids automatic retries for that reason: measure, find the source, quarantine visibly, fix. The app retries only failures that carry no verdict.

choices.text: Both are retries of a transient failure, so the pipeline should wait a random time between tries, as the app's jitter does
choices.why: Jitter spreads many clients so that a recovering server is not hit all at once. A test run is one client, and its failure is not a server asking for time.

choices.text: Retrying a test is acceptable once its random seed is fixed, because a fixed seed makes the third try behave exactly like the first
choices.why: Fixing a seed freezes an accident: the lesson's flaky test passed ten times with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` while still asserting an order the code never promised.

choices.text: Retries suit the pipeline and not the app, because a 503 retried by thousands of phones at once is a thundering herd
choices.why: The herd is why the app adds jitter, not a reason to stop retrying a 503. And a retried test hides a real failure, the opposite of what the app's retry does.

prompt: The planner's purchases server keeps the answer to each `Idempotency-Key` in a `Map` in memory, and every deploy to it is a recreate: stop the old process, start the new one. A phone's purchase loses its answer, and the retry arrives after a deploy. What happens?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 10; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 10.

choices.text: The retry lands in the recreate's gap, gets no answer at all, and is tried again until the new process sends back the saved answer
choices.why: The new process saved nothing. When the retry does get through, it is a key the server has never seen, sent to an empty `Map`.

choices.text: The server answers 409, since the key was still marked as in progress at the moment the old process stopped
choices.why: In progress was a state in the old process's memory, gone with it. The new one has no record of the key at all.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong, because the purchases server keeps a key for 24 hours and a deploy takes about a second
choices.why: The 24 hours is how long a running server keeps a key. A restart ends that early, whatever the clock says.

choices.text: The new process has never seen the key and charges the card again; keys belong in the purchases' database
choices.why: A restart forgets every key held in memory. The lesson keeps them beside the purchases for the reason the outbox row is written with its change: the two must never disagree.

prompt: Bia's test of the planner's pull plays two phones: phone B, whose clock is ten minutes slow, adds a session after phone A's last pull, and phone A asks the server for changes stamped after that pull. The session never arrives and the test fails. A teammate wants to give both fake phones the same clock so the test is deterministic. What do the two courses say?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 11; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 3.

choices.text: Align the clocks: a test that depends on the clock is flaky, and the testing course's cure for flakiness from time is to control it
choices.why: Controlling time means passing it in, which this test already does, and it fails every time. Aligning the clocks removes the very situation real phones are in.

choices.text: The test has found a real bug: a sync by the phone's stamp loses that session, and the fix is a server cursor
choices.why: Taking the clock as an input is what makes a test repeat. The skew is the case worth testing: a write stamped before a pull it came after is left out of every question asked by time.

choices.text: Quarantine the test in a separate, non-blocking job with an owner, as the testing course advises for flaky tests
choices.why: Quarantine is for a test that passes and fails with no change in between. This one fails every time, for a reason the sync lesson names.

choices.text: Keep the skew and have the phone stamp each session in the server's time zone, which takes the ten minutes out of the comparison
choices.why: A time zone does not repair a clock that is ten minutes slow; the stamp is still the phone's reckoning. Stamping on the server, or a cursor, takes the phone's clock out of the decision.

prompt: A pull is answered with 410 Gone, and the planner rebuilds its copy from scratch. Put the resync in order.
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 12.
items: Download the server's snapshot, with the cursor that goes with it
Write the snapshot into a new file beside the old database
Copy the outbox across and apply each pending operation to the new copy
Close both databases
Rename the new file over the old one
trap: The likeliest slip is leaving the outbox behind in the old file. The rename then throws away the person's unsent work, the one thing the server cannot send back.

prompt: The planner moves its last-write-wins stamp from the phone's clock to the server's, stamping each write when it arrives. Ana's phone changed a session from 20 to 30 minutes offline on a train at 10:05; her tablet ticked the same session done at 10:20, at home, and synced at 10:40; the phone found a network at 11:00. What does the server keep, and what does the lesson take from it?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 13.

choices.text: 20 minutes and done: the tablet's edit was made later, at 10:20, and the server's clock keeps the later edit
choices.why: The server's clock does not know when an edit was made, only when it arrived. The phone arrived at 11:00, and its copy replaced the row.

choices.text: 30 minutes and done: with the server's clock the skew is gone, and both edits survive
choices.why: The skew is gone, but last write wins still replaces the whole row. The phone's copy said not done, and it won.

choices.text: 30 minutes and not done: the phone arrived last, so its whole row won and the tick was lost; the server's clock measures connectivity, not intent
choices.why: Stamping on arrival ends the problem of a wrong clock, and the answer is still arbitrary. On another morning the tablet syncs last and the other field goes.

choices.text: Both copies are refused with a 409, because the server sees two writes to one row
choices.why: That is the check a version number makes, in the next lesson. Last write wins needs nothing but a stamp, and always produces an answer.

prompt: Match each piece of the planner's data to the way the conflict lessons settle two concurrent offline changes to it.
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 15.

pairs.left: a course's tags, where one device adds `exam` while the other removes `weekly`
the minutes studied this month, added to on both devices
a session whose length changed on the phone and whose tick changed on the tablet
pairs.right: a version number and a merge field by field

pairs.left: notes on the week, typed at the same place on both devices
pairs.right: a CRDT library for lists and text

pairs.left: a session's length, changed to two different values on two devices
pairs.right: keep both values and ask the person

right_distractors: lock the row until the other device syncs
a full resync from the server

prompt: The planner's sync tests use a stub server whose 409 body carries `current`, the row the server holds, which the merge reads. The server team renames that field to `latest`. Which tests notice?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 2; Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 14.

choices.text: None of the stubbed ones; a contract test that makes the real server answer 409 fails, which is what it exists for
choices.why: A stub says what the server answered when somebody wrote it, and goes on saying it. Only a test against the real thing sees that the merge now gets no row to merge against.

choices.text: The stubbed tests, since the merge reads `current` and the stub's answer no longer matches the server's code
choices.why: The stub's answer is written in the test, not read from the server. It still says `current`, so those tests stay green.

choices.text: The server's own functional tests, which fail on any change to the body of a response it sends to its clients
choices.why: The server's tests were changed together with the server, so they expect `latest` and pass. The disagreement is between two teams' assumptions.

choices.text: None, and none could, because a 409 happens only when two real devices edit the same row while both of them are offline at once
choices.why: A test can cause a 409 on purpose, as the version lesson did with two `curl` calls, the second naming a version the server had passed.

prompt: Ana writes property-based tests for the planner's grow-only counter of minutes, generating counter states for three devices. Which of these should hold for every generated input? Choose all that apply.
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 15; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 3.

choices.text: Merging A into B gives the same state as merging B into A
choices.why: Commutative: devices sync in whatever order they happen to find a network.

choices.text: The merged total equals the larger of the two totals
choices.why: The merge keeps the larger count for each device, and the total is the sum of those. The lesson's phone at 130 and tablet at 145 merge to 175.

choices.text: Merging A with B and then C gives what A merged with the merge of B and C gives
choices.why: Associative: updates may travel through other devices, in groups.

choices.text: Merging in a state that was already merged in changes nothing
choices.why: Idempotent: retries deliver some updates more than once.

choices.text: The merged state takes the counts of the device whose update arrived last
choices.why: That is last write wins, the rule that lost 45 minutes. Each device's entry takes the larger count, whichever arrived last.

prompt: In the background-sync lab, `node bg.ts 3 2` sends itself `SIGKILL` during its second step, the way a phone ends an app that overruns. A CI job runs that command as a step, to prepare the resume test. What exit status does the shell report for it?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 16; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5.

prompt: How should the planner's test suite check that the app survives the system emptying its cache folder, which both platforms are allowed to do?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 17; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 3.

choices.text: Mock the file system so that every read of the cache returns its last value, and assert that the screen draws what it got
choices.why: That tests the opposite case, a cache that never vanishes. The behaviour to prove is what happens when the read finds nothing.

choices.text: Point the tests at the app's real cache folder on the developer's machine, and empty it with `rm -rf` before each run
choices.why: A fixed, shared path is what a per-test temporary directory replaces: the next run or another test trips over it, and a real folder may hold something somebody needed.

choices.text: Nothing needs a test once the source of truth is kept out of the cache, because the system deletes only copies
choices.why: Keeping the truth elsewhere makes the loss harmless only if the code treats every read of the cache as one that may find nothing, and that is the part to test.

choices.text: Give the cache a fresh temporary directory, fill it, delete it, and run the screen: it must miss and fetch again
choices.why: The cache lesson says the technique is small enough to test that way, and a temporary directory per test keeps the deletion away from anything another test or a person needs.

prompt: The planner saves a downloaded 30 MB attachment so that a full disk leaves nothing half done. Put the steps in order.
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 18.
items: Ask how much room there is, for about twice the file's size
Write the bytes to a part file with a name of its own
Force the part file to storage with `fsync`
Rename the part file to its real name
Insert the row that records the file
trap: The likeliest slip is inserting the row before the rename. A disk that runs out after that leaves a row promising a whole file where there is two thirds of a PDF.

prompt: The planner shows a fingerprint prompt and, on `success: true`, opens its encrypted notes with a data key the app could already unwrap. What is wrong with that design?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 19.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the notes are sealed with AES-256-GCM, which refuses to open a file in which a single bit was changed
choices.why: GCM keeps an altered file from opening. It does nothing about a key the app could unwrap without any check at all.

choices.text: Passing the check releases nothing: code running as the app, or a debugger on a rooted phone, flips the boolean or skips it
choices.why: The key was usable all along, so the prompt is a curtain. Created to work only after a biometric check, the key itself becomes the lock.

choices.text: The data key should sit beside the notes, so that a backup restored to another phone still opens them
choices.why: A key beside its data is a lock with the key taped to it, and the lesson keeps the wrapping key on the phone that made it on purpose.

choices.text: A biometric should never guard data at all; the lesson keeps it for confirming a step that the server checks again
choices.why: A biometric that releases a key is the lesson's design for the data. The boolean is fine only in front of something the server checks again.

prompt: The planner's key for a paid tips service is stored as a CI secret, masked in every log, and the build writes it into the app's configuration so the app can call the service directly. The logs show `***`. How safe is the key?
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 20; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.

choices.text: Safe, because the CI store encrypts it and masking keeps the value out of every place a person could read it
choices.why: Masking covers the job logs. The bundle that ships to every phone carries the value as it is, and a search for its shape finds it.

choices.text: Safe once the build stores it in base64, which neither a person reading the bundle nor the masking would recognise
choices.why: Encoding changes the command somebody types to find the key, and nothing else. It also defeats the log masking, which matches only the exact value.

choices.text: It is published: anything compiled into the bundle is readable by whoever downloads the app
choices.why: Masking keeps a value out of the pipeline's logs. The bundle has a different audience, everybody with the app, and the only fix is an app that never holds the key.

choices.text: Unsafe only on a rooted phone, so encrypting the configuration with a key from the keystore closes the gap
choices.why: The app has to use the key, so it has to be able to decrypt it, and so can whoever holds the app. No encryption on the device rescues a secret the app must read.

prompt: The planner is filling in Google Play's Data safety form and Apple's App Privacy details. Which of these have to be declared as collected? Choose all that apply.
hint: Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 20.

choices.text: Sessions the outbox sends to the planner's server
choices.why: Once data leaves the device it is collected, and it goes on the form.

choices.text: Sessions in a copy of the planner that never syncs them anywhere
choices.why: Data processed only on the device and never sent off it is not collected, in both stores' terms.

choices.text: The device model a crash-reporting library sends with every report
choices.why: Both stores count data a library collects as data the app collects.

choices.text: The e-mail address the server uses to sign the person in
choices.why: It is sent to the planner's server, so it is collected, whatever the device keeps after sign-in.

choices.text: The theme the person chose, kept in key-value storage on the phone
choices.why: A setting that never leaves the device is not collected.

prompt: After the planner's leaked log line, the pipeline gains a step that runs `grep` for anything shaped like an e-mail address over the logs the test suite produced. It finds nothing. What has it shown?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 6; Data on the Device: Offline, Sync and Conflicts, lesson 20.

choices.text: That the logs are free of personal data, since an address is the most identifying thing a log line could carry
choices.why: The leaked line also carried a name and a note about an exam. And a line the app writes only in production never passes through the suite.

choices.text: Nothing of use, because a `grep` cannot stand in for a person reviewing every log line before a release
choices.why: A `grep` in the pipeline runs on every change, which no review does. Its limit is what it looks for, not that a machine runs it.

choices.text: That the crash reporter can be declared in the store forms as a library that collects nothing at all about the person
choices.why: The forms ask what the app and its libraries send, and a crash reporter sends data of its own, the device's model among it, whatever the app's own lines say.

choices.text: That the mistake it was written for is not in those logs, and nothing more: finding nothing is no proof of nothing
choices.why: The pattern reliably finds an address in a log line. It cannot see a name, a note about an exam, or a line no test made the app write.

prompt: In `shipquote`, 24 unit tests take 0.17 seconds and the other 7 take 1.21. `--durations` shows that the two slowest entries are teardowns of 0.50 seconds each. Where did most of the top layers' time go?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 1.

choices.text: Shutting down the HTTP server the functional tests share, which waits up to half a second for each module that uses it
choices.why: `serve_forever` checks for a shutdown every half second, and the fixture is torn down once per module. The requests themselves took hundredths of a second.

choices.text: The HTTP requests, since a functional test sends real requests over a socket where a unit test only calls a function
choices.why: The whole acceptance test, six quotes included, took 0.03 seconds. The cost is building and removing the world the test runs in.

choices.text: Creating a fresh SQLite database for each functional test, which the store fixture does test by test
choices.why: The store fixture serves the integration tests, and SQLite in the same process costs almost nothing. The teardowns listed are the server's.

choices.text: pytest collecting the 31 tests again, which it does once for every marker expression in the run
choices.why: Collecting the whole suite takes about a tenth of a second, and the slowest entries listed are teardowns, not collection.

prompt: A place in the code where a collaborator is handed in, rather than built inside the function that uses it, is what lets a test pass a double. The lesson calls that place a ___.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 2.

prompt: `shipquote`'s coverage report misses `main()`, which reads `SHIPQUOTE_PORT` and starts the server, and the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard that calls it. The team adds an exclusion for one of them. Which, and why?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 4.

choices.text: Both, because code that only runs in a deployment cannot be tested and only adds noise to the list of missing lines
choices.why: It can be checked, by the smoke test against the deployed program. Excluding it would take it off the list before anything checked it.

choices.text: Neither, because every exclusion is the threshold game played with configuration instead of tests
choices.why: Used broadly it is. The guard is a line nothing should test, and keeping it only adds noise to the list a reader checks.

choices.text: Only the guard: `main()` stays counted, because a mistake in it is a real bug and the check that covers it is the smoke test after a deploy
choices.why: Excluding `main()` would hide it from the one report showing it is not yet checked anywhere. A typo in the variable's name or a server bound to the wrong address are the bugs that live there.

choices.text: Only `main()`, with `# pragma: no cover`, since the guard already runs every time the module is imported
choices.why: The guard's body runs only when the file is run as a program, which the tests never do. And `main()` is the part with something in it to check.

prompt: When one cell of a GitHub Actions matrix goes red, the service cancels the cells still running unless the workflow sets `strategy.___: false`. Run 4's pattern, every UTC cell red and every São Paulo cell green, needed every cell to finish.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5.

prompt: Which of these pipeline steps end green while having checked nothing they were meant to check? Choose all that apply.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5.

choices.text: `python -m pytest -q -m smoke | tee run.log`, in a shell without `pipefail`, where no test carries `smoke`
choices.why: pytest exits 5 when it ran nothing, and the pipe reports `tee`'s 0.

choices.text: The same pytest command, in a step that begins with `set -euo pipefail`
choices.why: `pipefail` hands the pipe pytest's 5, and the step fails, as it should.

choices.text: `coverage report --fail-under=85 | tail -1`, with coverage at 81%
choices.why: The failure message is printed, and the status is `tail`'s, which succeeded.

choices.text: A job running the contract tests where `CARRIER_URL` is never set
choices.why: Both tests are skipped and the run reports success. A skipped test is not a passing test.

choices.text: A required check on a workflow filtered by `paths:`, for a pull request that changes only the README
choices.why: That workflow never runs and reports nothing, so the pull request waits for ever. It is stuck, not green.

prompt: Which of these belong in the smoke test `shipquote` runs against production right after every deploy? Choose all that apply.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7.

choices.text: Placing a test order, to prove the whole checkout works end to end
choices.why: Nothing that writes data a customer could see belongs there.

choices.text: Asking `/health` and expecting it to answer `ok`
choices.why: Is it up: the first of the two questions that matter first.

choices.text: Asking `/version` and expecting the version the artifact's name promised
choices.why: Is it the version we meant: a restart that did not happen would answer as the old one.

choices.text: One quote for a known CEP, a real read through the main path
choices.why: It proves the program can do its job and not only answer `/health`, and it writes nothing.

choices.text: A price asked of the paid carrier, to prove the integration answers
choices.why: Nothing that costs money belongs in a check that runs after every deploy.

prompt: The planner's server has to rename the `minutes` column of its sessions table to `duration`, while the release before each new one keeps running against the same database during every deploy. Put the releases in the order that keeps each step safe to roll back.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7.
items: Add the new column `duration` beside `minutes`
Release code that writes both columns and still reads `minutes`
Copy `minutes` into `duration` for the rows written before
Release code that reads `duration`
Stop writing `minutes`, and drop it in a later release
trap: The likeliest slip is dropping `minutes` in the release that starts reading `duration`. The release before it still reads `minutes`, so the rollback the steps exist to protect would fail.

prompt: Which of these leave `shipquote`'s carrier token readable by people who should not have it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.

choices.text: A commit that added it, removed by the next commit twenty minutes later
choices.why: The history keeps it: `git log -S` finds both commits, and `git show` prints the file with the token in it.

choices.text: A `config.env` holding it with the default permissions `-rw-r--r--`
choices.why: Every other user on the machine can read that file. `chmod 600` leaves it to the owner.

choices.text: An environment variable, set by the script that starts the process
choices.why: A process's environment is readable by its owner and by root only, which is why the lab hands the token over that way.

choices.text: Starting the program with `--carrier-token=` among its arguments
choices.why: On Linux any user can list every process's arguments with `ps`.

choices.text: A job log in which the token was printed exactly as registered, with masking on
choices.why: Masking replaces the exact value before the line is stored. What gets through is the value encoded, split or partly printed.

prompt: Release 1.6.1 reached production with the delivery estimate behind a flag set for nobody: the new code ran on every request and no customer saw it. Deploying code switched off in this way is sometimes called a ___ launch.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 10.

prompt: A canary release fails one request in twenty of the shop's usual mix. By the lesson's arithmetic, how many requests must reach the canary before the chance of seeing at least one error reaches 95%?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 10.

prompt: `shipquote` sets an objective that 99.9% of quote requests succeed over 30 days, and it serves two million requests a month. How many failed requests does its error budget allow in that month?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11.

prompt: Ana pushed a commit that added the planner's `upload.jks` to the shared repository, and noticed an hour later. The planner uses Play App Signing. What comes first?
hint: Publishing and Operating a Mobile App, lesson 1; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: Generate a new app signing key and sign the next release with it, so phones stop trusting the leaked one
choices.why: The key that leaked is the upload key; phones only ever check the one Google holds. A new key on the same package name is an update every phone refuses.

choices.text: Run `git rm --cached upload.jks`, add `*.jks` to `.gitignore` and push, which takes the keystore out of the shared copy
choices.why: Deleting a file does not change the commit that added it. `git show` on that commit still prints the keystore, in every clone made since.

choices.text: Treat the key as public: the account owner asks for an upload key reset and registers a new upload certificate
choices.why: Replacing the secret is the only step that fixes anything once it is in a pushed commit. It is the upload key, so a reset costs nothing on any phone.

choices.text: Rewrite the history with `git filter-repo` and have everybody clone again; then the same key is safe to keep
choices.why: Rewriting removes the file from the history from now on, and does not undo the copies somebody already made. The key has to be treated as public whatever the history says.

prompt: A crash from the planner's 1.5.0 arrives with frames such as `a.b`, and the release's `mapping.txt` was never kept. Bruno checks out the tag `v1.5.0`, builds the release again, and runs retrace with the new mapping. What should he expect?
hint: Publishing and Operating a Mobile App, lesson 13; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 7.

choices.text: Nothing to trust: the rebuild's short names and inlining are its own, so retrace prints confident nonsense
choices.why: Only the file produced by the build that shipped undoes that build's rewriting. That is why the mapping is kept and uploaded with every release.

choices.text: The original trace, because a tag does not move and one commit gives one mapping
choices.why: The tag fixes the source, not what a build does with it. Two builds of the same commit can choose different short names and different inlining.

choices.text: A refusal from retrace saying the mapping belongs to another build, the way a dSYM with another UUID is refused
choices.why: Refusing a mismatched file is the dSYM's behaviour. The lesson says the wrong build's mapping makes the same command print confident nonsense.

choices.text: The original trace, as long as the new build carries the same version code, 1050003
choices.why: The version code names the build for the stores and the crash reporter. It does not decide which names R8 picks.

prompt: The planner's repository is kept the Git Flow way, and 1.5.0 is live in both stores. A bug turns up that people on the 1.4 line report too. Bruno proposes a branch from the `v1.4.0` tag, released as 1.4.1. What do the two lessons say?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 9; Publishing and Operating a Mobile App, lesson 9.

choices.text: Release 1.4.1: its version code is new, and Google Play only refuses a code it has seen before
choices.why: Production already holds 1.5.0's higher code, so Play refuses 1.4.1 there, and a phone on 1.5.0 would never accept it either.

choices.text: Start `hotfix/1.5.1` from `main`, which holds 1.5.0: phone versions only move forward
choices.why: A Git Flow hotfix starts from `main`, where only released versions are. On a phone there is one line of versions and it only moves forward, so the fix is 1.5.1.

choices.text: Release 1.4.1, since the stores compare the version name, and 1.4.1 is a new one
choices.why: The name is shown and never compared. Android decides about an update by the version code alone, and 1.4.1's is lower than 1.5.0's.

choices.text: Start the fix from `develop`, so it reaches people as part of 1.6.0 with the next features
choices.why: In Git Flow a fix to a released version starts from `main` so that it does not wait for the next release's features.

prompt: Ana tags the release commit with `git tag -a v1.5.0 -m "Release 1.5.0"` and runs `git push`. The planner's release workflow starts on a pushed tag that matches `v*`, yet no release run appears. Why?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 7; Publishing and Operating a Mobile App, lesson 10.

choices.text: The workflow reacts to lightweight tags, and `-a` made an annotated tag, an object of its own
choices.why: Annotated tags are the ones lesson 7 recommends for a release. The run never started because the tag never left Ana's machine.

choices.text: The tag reached the shared copy, and the run waits for somebody to promote it from the internal track
choices.why: A promotion moves a build that was already uploaded. Here nothing was built, because no tag arrived to start a build.

choices.text: The build jobs run on the next morning's schedule, which picks up every tag pushed since the last one
